1.title: The Night the Lights Went Out
1.topic: Reconstructing what happened — and what used to happen
1.focus: Simple past: ordinary verbs and the verb “to be”

lines.text: Owen, were you at home during the blackout last Thursday?
Yes, I was. I was alone in the flat. Suddenly, at about nine o'clock, all the lights went off.
What did you do?
At first, I didn't notice anything strange, because I was asleep on the sofa. Then I woke up and everything was dark.
Were you scared?
A little. I couldn't find my phone. I looked everywhere, and finally I found it under a cushion.
Did you call anyone?
I called my neighbour, Mrs Ortiz. She was fine. She lit some candles and invited me for tea.
That was nice of her. How long did the blackout last?
About three hours. The electricity came back at midnight.
What happened? Did they explain it?
Yes. The news said a big tree fell on the power lines near the river.
Wow. I was in Medellín at the time, so I missed it all.

questions.explain_es: Owen dice: 'About three hours.'

questions.explain_es: Owen dice: 'finally I found it under a cushion.'

questions.q: Why did the blackout happen?
options: A tree fell on the power lines.
The neighbours used too much electricity.
questions.explain_es: Owen dice: 'The news said a big tree fell on the power lines near the river.'

questions.q: Where was Laura during the blackout?
questions.explain_es: Laura dice: 'I was in Medellín at the time, so I missed it all.'

questions.q: Owen noticed the blackout immediately.
questions.explain_es: Falso. Owen dice: 'At first, I didn't notice anything strange, because I was asleep on the sofa.'

questions.explain_es: Verdadero. Owen dice: 'She lit some candles and invited me for tea.'

questions.explain_es: 'Come' es irregular: el pasado es 'came'. Owen dice: 'The electricity came back at midnight.'

1.title: From the Bank to the Beach
1.topic: Reconstructing what happened — and what used to happen
1.focus: Past habits and states with “used to”

lines.text: Rocío, ten years ago you worked in a bank in Bogotá. What was your life like back then?
Very different! I used to get up at five and take two buses to the office.
Did you like the job?
Not really. I used to wear a suit every day, and I didn't use to see the sun much.
So why did you quit?
One day, I visited Nuquí, on the Pacific coast, for a holiday. I fell in love with the ocean.
And then you moved house?
Yes. Three months later, I moved to Nuquí and opened a small surf school.
Did you use to surf as a child?
No, I didn't. I used to be afraid of the water! I learned when I was thirty.
How do you look back on your old life now?
I don't miss it. At the time, I thought a bank job was safe. Now I know that happiness is more important.

2.title: The Office Kitchen

lines.text: Tim, I'm making the shopping list for the office kitchen. Can you check the cupboards?
Sure. OK, we have plenty of coffee. There are three big bags.
Good. How much sugar is there?
Not much. There's only a little in the container. We need more.
And tea? Do we have enough tea bags?
We have a few, but not enough for the whole week. Maybe ten.
OK, tea bags. What about milk?
There isn't any milk. We ran out of it yesterday.
Right. How many cups are there? Last week a couple of them broke.
There are lots of cups, but there aren't many spoons. Only four!
People always take the spoons to their desks. Anything else?
There's a large amount of biscuits. I don't think anyone likes them.
Ha! Then we don't need any biscuits this time.

lines.text: So, Nadia, which rehearsal room do you prefer? The one in Chapinero or the one in Teusaquillo?

Yes, but the Teusaquillo room is twice as big, and it's not as expensive.
How much is it?
Forty thousand pesos an hour. The Chapinero room costs sixty thousand.
Hmm. The only drawback is the noise. The neighbours in Teusaquillo complain a lot.
Really? Is it too noisy for them?
Yes. We can only play until eight o'clock. That isn't late enough for us.
I see. And the equipment? Is it decent?
The Teusaquillo room has better speakers. The Chapinero ones aren't as good.
OK. I think we can put up with the eight o'clock rule. Let's book Teusaquillo.

4.title: My First Half Marathon

lines.text: Hello, and welcome to Run Club Radio. I'm Sara, and today I want to tell you about my first half marathon.

7.title: Working from Home: Five Tips

lines.text: Hello, I'm Megan, and welcome to Work Smart. Today: how to work from home without going crazy.
Tip number one: get dressed. Don't work in your pyjamas. It's a good idea to feel ready for the day.
Tip number two: make sure you have a quiet place to work. Avoid working in bed or on the sofa.
Tip number three: take short breaks. Stand up every hour in order to rest your eyes and your back.
Tip number four: turn off notifications on your phone. The best way to concentrate is to put it in another room.
Tip number five: keep moving. Go for a walk at lunchtime, even for ten minutes.
And remember to finish at a fixed time. Close your laptop at six and don't open it again!
Many listeners have written to us about this. One listener, Andrés from Barranquilla, says the walk at lunchtime is the most useful tip.
Try these ideas for a week and tell us what happens.

11.title: How Panela Is Made
11.topic: When the action matters more than the actor

lines.text: Welcome to How It's Made, the podcast about everyday things. I'm Simon. Today we're visiting a trapiche in Santander, where panela is produced.
Panela is a type of brown sugar. It's eaten all over Colombia, and it's used to make aguapanela, a very popular hot drink.
First, the sugar cane is cut by hand in the fields.
Then the cane is carried to the trapiche by mules or by truck.
There, the juice is taken out of the cane by a big machine.
Next, the juice is boiled in large pots for several hours. A lot of heat is required, so the fire is never allowed to go out.
The thick liquid is poured into moulds. In about twenty minutes, it becomes hard.
After that, the blocks of panela are wrapped in paper or plastic.
Finally, they're delivered to shops and supermarkets around the country.
More than one million tonnes of panela are produced in Colombia every year.
Next week: how chocolate is made. See you then!

14.title: A Noise in the Kitchen
14.topic: How sure you are, and what you are allowed to do
14.focus: Modals and adverbs for degrees of certainty

lines.text: Ahmed, wake up! Can you hear that noise? It's coming from the kitchen.
Hmm... It's probably the cat.
It can't be the cat. The cat is sleeping on my bed.
Then it might be the wind. The window was open this evening.
No, I closed it before dinner. I'm certain.
OK. Perhaps it's our neighbour, Mr Díaz. He sometimes comes in to borrow sugar.
At two in the morning? That's very unlikely.
You're right. Let's go and see. Bring your phone.
Look! The fridge door is open and there's cheese on the floor.
And there are small footprints everywhere. They must be from an animal.
There! Under the table! It's an opossum!
Wow. It must be really hungry. It ate all our cheese!
We're not allowed to keep pets in this building, so let's open the door and let it go.

questions.explain_es: Carla dice: 'The cat is sleeping on my bed.'

questions.explain_es: Carla dice: 'It's an opossum!'

questions.explain_es: 'Might' = es posible, pero no seguro. Ahmed dice: 'Then it might be the wind.'

questions.explain_es: 'Must be' = estoy casi seguro (por la evidencia). Ahmed dice: 'They must be from an animal.'

14.title: Airport Security Information
14.topic: How sure you are, and what you are allowed to do

lines.text: Good morning, passengers. Welcome to El Dorado International Airport. Please listen carefully to the following security information.
You are allowed to carry liquids in your hand luggage, but each bottle must be one hundred millilitres or less.
All liquids have to be in a clear plastic bag.
Sharp objects, like knives and scissors, are strictly prohibited in the cabin.
You are supposed to take your laptop out of your bag at the security check.
You don't have to take off your shoes, unless the officer asks you to.
Smoking is forbidden everywhere in the airport, including the bathrooms.
Passengers are not allowed to leave bags without someone watching them. Unattended bags will be removed.
Please remember that international passengers are supposed to arrive three hours before their flight.
Domestic passengers should arrive at least two hours before.
Thank you, and have a pleasant journey.

15.title: If I Were the Mayor
15.topic: Imaginary situations and things you should have done differently
15.focus: Unreal conditional sentences with if clauses (second conditional)

lines.text: Charlotte, if you were the mayor of Bogotá, what would you change first?
If I were the mayor, I would build more bike lanes. The traffic is terrible.
Good idea. I would plant more trees. If there were more trees, the air would be cleaner.
And what would you do about the buses?
I'd buy electric buses. They'd be quieter, and they wouldn't pollute the city.
But they're very expensive. Where would you get the money?
Hmm. If drivers paid a small tax of five thousand pesos to drive in the centre, we'd have enough money.
Drivers wouldn't be happy! I think you'd lose the next election.
Maybe. But in my shoes, what would you do?
I'd do the same, actually. And I'd make the museums free on Sundays.
Some museums are already free on Sundays.
Really? I didn't know that. Then I'd make the buses free every Sunday!

15.title: Lessons Learned
15.topic: Imaginary situations and things you should have done differently
15.focus: Past modals: should have and would have

lines.text: Welcome to Lessons Learned, the podcast about mistakes. My guest today is Andrés Vargas. Andrés, tell us about your biggest mistake.
Five years ago, I opened a restaurant in Cali. After eight months, I had to close it.
What went wrong?
I chose a bad location. I should have looked at more places first. There weren't many people on that street.
Did anyone warn you?
Yes, my father did. I should have listened to him, but I was too excited.
What would you have done differently?
I would have started with a food truck instead. It's much cheaper, and you can move it.
Do you blame yourself?
Not anymore. In hindsight, it was a great lesson. Now I have two successful food trucks.
So, what's your advice for our listeners?
Don't turn down good advice. And don't spend all your money on day one!

16.title: After the Interview
16.topic: Passing on what other people said and asked for

lines.text: Isa! How was the job interview? What did they say?
It went well, I think! The manager, Mrs Clark, said that the company was growing fast.
That's good news. What else did she say?
She said they needed someone who spoke English and Portuguese. I mentioned that I had lived in Brazil for a year.
Did she talk about money?
Yes. She told me the salary was four million pesos a month.
Wow! Did she say when they would decide?
She said she would call me by Friday. She also mentioned that there were two other candidates.
Two? Did she say anything about them?
Not really. But she admitted that I was the only one with experience in tourism.
Apparently you made a good impression, then.
I hope so! She promised that she would send me an email with more information today.
